title: KONA BLUE (2011)

lead.text: KONA BLUE was a proposed special access programme at the Department of Homeland Security, established as a prospective programme in 2011 and terminated in February 2012 without ever being approved. AARO says its advocates proposed to reverse-engineer any off-world spacecraft they hoped to acquire and to move alleged programmes' technology under it for oversight, and that the material was only assumed to exist.

summary.text: The origin, as AARO tells it: after DIA ended AAWSAP/AATIP, its supporters proposed that DHS create and fund a new version under a special access programme, with lines of effort mirroring the private contractor's AAWSAP work.

The paper trail: the DHS Science and Technology Under Secretary established it as a prospective programme, the Deputy Secretary terminated it about six months later, and DHS declassified the file in February 2024; AARO and DHS published it in June 2024.

The dispute: AARO's Volume I offers KONA BLUE as the rejected proposal that witnesses mistook for an operating programme, while the proposal's own premise, moving concealed holdings under oversight, assumes the holdings existed.

record.text: The joint AARO and DHS paper states that in 2011 the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology established KONA BLUE as a prospective special access programme, and that the Deputy Secretary disapproved and terminated it about six months later; it was never approved or formally established, and neither official is named in the released text.

DHS records the programme as terminated on 10 February 2012; its Acting Deputy Secretary transmitted the declassified records to the Deputy Secretary of Defense on 5 February 2024, and AARO published the package in June 2024.

AARO's Volume I says the proposal would restart UAP investigations and paranormal research and reverse-engineer any recovered off-world spacecraft its proponents hoped to acquire, and included an oral history initiative to gather information on the location of advanced aerospace technology and biological samples from a list of retired officials, officers and contractors.

AARO records that Senators Lieberman and Reid asked that the programme be established with the promise of additional funding, and that proponents believed a DHS programme would let the technology of the alleged programmes be moved under KONA BLUE where oversight committees could monitor it.
AARO states that KONA BLUE was not reported to Congress at the time because it was never established as a special access programme and so did not meet the threshold for reporting.

The background is on record: at Reid's direction Congress appropriated $22 million for DIA's AAWSAP in fiscal 2008 and 2010, the sole bidder was Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies, and the programme was terminated in 2012. AARO refers to KONA BLUE's anticipated contract performers without naming them; the board reads this as Bigelow's organisation.

In June 2009 Reid wrote to the Deputy Secretary of Defense asking for a restricted special access programme with a bigoted access list over parts of the programme, citing several highly sensitive, unconventional aerospace-related findings. DIA prepared to tell him in November 2009 that the deliverables did not meet the criteria for a special access programme. DoD confirmed the letter authentic in 2019.

claimed.text: The interviewees who brought KONA BLUE to AARO claimed it was a sensitive DHS compartment to cover up the retrieval and exploitation of non-human biologics.
Reporting on the document releases identifies the DHS Under Secretary for Science and Technology who set it up as Tara O'Toole; the released paper withholds the name.
James Lacatski hinted to Jeremy Corbell in April 2026 that a smaller, more focused effort related to KONA BLUE continued after AAWSAP ended.

UAP Gerb told NewsNation in August 2026 that KONA BLUE was a DHS-brokered programme in which Lockheed Martin material was diverted before the CIA shut it down; the episode set it beside the Immaculate Constellation document and Matthew Brown's claims.

George Knapp testified in September 2025 that Bigelow and an AAWSAP colleague negotiated with senior Lockheed Martin executives for unusual material held at a facility in California, and Luis Elizondo told the House in November 2024 that the transfer was blocked. No record ties this transfer to KONA BLUE beyond UAP Gerb's account.

The board infers that a proposal to protect the retrieval and exploitation of non-human biologics is only drafted by people who believe such material exists and is held somewhere, which AARO's own wording concedes while saying they were wrong.

contested.text: AARO states that DHS leadership rejected the proposal for lacking merit, that it was never stood up, and that no extraterrestrial craft or bodies were ever collected: the material was only assumed to exist by KONA BLUE advocates and its anticipated contract performers.

AARO's sequence does not fit the DHS dates: AARO says supporters turned to DHS after DIA cancelled AAWSAP/AATIP in 2012, but the DHS paper says KONA BLUE was established in 2011 and the DHS letter dates its termination to 10 February 2012.

AARO attributes the reverse-engineering claims largely to circular reporting among a group of individuals active since 2009, says none of its interviewees had firsthand knowledge, and says it found no empirical evidence for them.
AARO says executives and technology chiefs of the companies interviewees named denied the programmes on the record; it names no company and describes no inspection of any facility or holding.

AARO is not a neutral source here. On the board's reading its lack-of-merit framing sits against DIA's own 2009 review of AAWSAP, which found the reviews positive, and it published a full package on this rejected proposal but none on the intelligence community programme it concedes was expanded in 2021 to a reverse-engineering mission.
Deputy Secretary Hicks declined to endorse Volume I's key findings publicly, and Christopher Mellon called them mid-level assertions without cabinet-level ratification.

On the board's reading the two readings cannot yet be told apart: AARO offers KONA BLUE as the misunderstanding that produced later allegations, while the alternative is that both are downstream of the same activity, and AARO has published no interview transcripts that would settle it.

questions: Who were the DHS Under Secretary who established KONA BLUE and the Deputy Secretary who terminated it, and what did their written determinations say?
What additional funding did Senators Lieberman and Reid promise, and through what vehicle?
Did any smaller effort related to KONA BLUE continue after 2012, as Lacatski hints?
Was any material ever delivered to Bigelow's company, and what was the facility in California?
Will AARO's promised Volume II, or the interview records behind Volume I, show whether KONA BLUE generated the later allegations or shared a source with them?
